sections.title: Core Concepts: Evolution
sections.instructions: Answer each question in full sentences unless a term is requested.
sections.stimulus: CAPS Grade 12 Term 3 focus: Diversity, Change and Continuity; Darwinism, natural selection and human evolution.

questions.question: Define biological evolution.
memo: Change in the inherited characteristics/genetic composition of populations over successive generations. Award 2 for population-level change over time.

questions.question: Distinguish between a scientific hypothesis and a scientific theory.
memo: Hypothesis: testable proposed explanation. Theory: well-supported explanation built from repeated evidence and testing.

questions.question: Explain why genetic variation is necessary for natural selection to occur.
memo: Individuals must differ in inherited traits; some variants give survival/reproductive advantage; advantageous alleles become more common.

questions.question: State TWO sources of genetic variation in a sexually reproducing population.
memo: Accept: mutation, crossing over, random arrangement/segregation of chromosomes, random fertilisation. Any two.

questions.question: Differentiate between homologous structures and analogous structures.
memo: Homologous: same basic structure/common ancestry but may have different functions. Analogous: similar function but different evolutionary origin/basic structure.

questions.question: Give THREE reasons why the fossil record is incomplete.
memo: Accept: not all organisms fossilise; soft parts decay; geological processes destroy fossils; fossils remain undiscovered; conditions for fossilisation are rare. Any three.

sections.title: Diagram Interpretation: Human Evolution
sections.instructions: Use Figure 3, the hominin skull comparison diagram.
sections.stimulus: Figure 3 shows two simplified skulls and three labelled features used as evidence in human evolution.

questions.question: Identify the labelled feature A and explain why it is useful when comparing hominin skulls.
memo: A is cranial capacity/brain case size; larger cranial capacity is associated with increased brain size in later hominins.

questions.question: Identify labelled feature B and state what a less projecting jaw suggests about diet or evolutionary trend.
memo: B is jaw projection/prognathism; reduced jaw projection suggests a flatter face and is generally associated with later hominins/changed diet and dentition.

questions.question: Identify labelled feature C and explain how its position is linked to bipedalism.
memo: C is foramen magnum; a more central/forward position under the skull indicates the skull balances on an upright vertebral column, supporting bipedalism.

questions.question: Which skull, A or B, is more likely to represent the more recent hominin? Give TWO visible reasons from the diagram.
memo: Skull B; accept larger cranial capacity/rounder cranium, flatter face/less projecting jaw, more central foramen magnum. Any two visible reasons.

questions.question: Name TWO other forms of evidence, besides skull anatomy, that scientists use to study human evolution.
memo: Accept: fossils of other bones, stone tools/artefacts, DNA/molecular evidence, comparative anatomy, dating methods, cultural evidence. Any two with explanation for full marks.

sections.title: Data Response: Natural Selection
sections.instructions: Use Figure 1, the finch beak depth table and graph.
sections.stimulus: Figure 1 summarises changes in rainfall, hard seed availability and mean beak depth in an island finch population.

questions.question: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable shown in the graph in Figure 1.
memo: Independent variable: year/time. Dependent variable: mean beak depth. Award credit for identifying rainfall/hard-seed availability as environmental variables in the table.

questions.question: Describe the trend in mean beak depth from 2019 to 2022.
memo: Mean beak depth increased steadily from 8.7 mm to 10.2 mm over the period. Must mention direction and data values/range.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage increase in mean beak depth from 2019 to 2022. Show all working.
memo: Increase = 10.2 - 8.7 = 1.5 mm; percentage increase = 1.5/8.7 x 100 = 17.24% or 17.2%. Award method marks.

questions.question: Use the data to explain how natural selection could have caused the change in mean beak depth.
memo: Drier years had lower rainfall and more hard seeds; birds varied in beak depth; deeper beaks cracked hard seeds more effectively; those birds survived/reproduced more; alleles for deeper beaks increased; population mean shifted.

questions.question: Predict what may happen to mean beak depth after several wet years with more soft seeds. Justify your answer.
memo: Mean beak depth may decrease or selection pressure may weaken; smaller/shallower beaks may no longer be disadvantaged when soft seeds are abundant. Accept well-reasoned alternatives.

sections.title: Investigation Design and Evaluation
sections.instructions: Use Figure 2, the investigation method and data sheet.
sections.stimulus: A learner investigates whether seed hardness affects feeding success in two finch-beak models.

questions.question: Write a suitable aim for this investigation.
memo: To determine the effect of seed hardness on feeding success/number of seeds collected by different beak models.

questions.question: Formulate a testable hypothesis for the investigation.
memo: Example: If seed hardness increases, then the model with the deeper/stronger beak will collect more seeds than the smaller beak model. Must link variables.

questions.question: Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and TWO controlled variables.
memo: Independent: seed hardness/type. Dependent: number/mass of seeds collected or feeding success. Controlled variables: time allowed, number of seeds, same surface/container, same model users, same number of trials.

questions.question: Give TWO ways to improve the reliability or validity of the investigation.
memo: Repeat trials/calculate averages; use same time for each trial; use equal seed numbers/masses; control technique; use larger sample; test one variable at a time.

questions.question: Write a conclusion that would be supported if the stronger beak model collected more hard seeds in every trial.
memo: The stronger/deeper beak model is better adapted to hard seeds; seed hardness affects feeding success; this supports selection for deeper beaks under hard-seed conditions.

questions.question: Explain why a larger sample size would make the results more trustworthy.
memo: A larger sample reduces the effect of chance/anomalies, gives more representative data, and increases confidence in the pattern/conclusion.
